subsection: 4. The Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act (1996)

notes.h: Purpose and scope of the Act
notes.b: The Act regulates the employment of young people so that work does not harm their health, safety or development.
points: The Act applies to young people who are employed, and sets the minimum age, working hours, breaks and rest entitlements for them.
A young person is generally under 18.
The Act sets out what employers must do before employing a young person, and what records they must keep.
It is an offence to employ a child under 16 on a full-time basis.
Children under 14 may not work during school term.
Young people aged 14 and over may do light work, such as during school holidays or approved work experience.
Children under 16 may take part in licensed work in film, theatre, sport or advertising, subject to licence conditions.
14- and 15-year-olds may do light work for up to 8 hours a week during school term.
During school holidays, 14- and 15-year-olds may work up to 35 hours a week.
14- and 15-year-olds must have at least 21 days off work during the summer holidays.
16- and 17-year-olds may work up to 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week.
14- and 15-year-olds must get a 30-minute break after 4 hours' work.
16- and 17-year-olds must get a 30-minute break after 4.5 hours' work.
Young workers must have rest days each week, normally two days in a row.
14- and 15-year-olds may not work between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m.
16- and 17-year-olds may not be required to work after 10 p.m. or before 6 a.m., with limited exceptions.
Before employing anyone under 18, the employer must see a copy of their birth certificate or other evidence of age.
For a young person under 16, the employer must have the written permission of a parent or guardian.
Employers must keep a register of each young person's age, hours worked and pay.
Employers who break the Act can be prosecuted and fined.

notes.h: Other legislation protecting people in employment
notes.b: The Act is one of several laws that protect workers. Their main areas are the following.
points: Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005: employers must assess risks and provide a safe workplace.
National Minimum Wage Act 2000: sets the lowest hourly rate an employer may pay, with lower rates for workers under 20.
Employment Equality Acts 1998–2015: prohibit discrimination at work on nine grounds, including gender, age, disability and race.
Organisation of Working Time Act 1997: limits adult working hours, sets rest breaks and gives paid annual leave.

keyTerms.definition: A person generally under 18 years of age who is employed, and protected by the Act.
Work that is permitted for those aged 14 and over, such as light holiday work or approved work experience, and is not harmful to health or development.
A day free of work that a young worker must receive each week.
A written record kept by an employer of the hours worked by each young person.
Permission from a parent or guardian, which an employer must obtain before employing a young person.
Work in film, theatre, sport or advertising by a child under 16, permitted only under a licence.
A placement arranged as part of education, which allows young people to work under agreed conditions.

factCards.term: Three employer obligations under the Act
factCards.definition: Obtain evidence of the young person's age; obtain permission from a parent or guardian; keep a register of the hours worked.
Licensed work in film, theatre, sport or advertising, and approved work experience.
Young workers are generally not permitted to work late at night or early in the morning.

factCards.term: Two protections on breaks and rest
factCards.definition: A break after a set period of work, with the length depending on age; a set number of rest days and free days each week.
To protect young people's health, safety and development by regulating their hours, breaks, rest and times of work.

factCards.term: Five areas of wider employment protection
factCards.definition: Health and safety; minimum pay; equality and discrimination; working time limits; leave and benefits.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which the Act limits the working hours of young people.
questions.model: The Act limits hours during school term for those aged 14 and 15, and sets a weekly limit that is lower for 15-year-olds. It limits holiday work to a maximum number of hours per day and per week. It also requires breaks during the working day and rest days each week.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act (1996) safeguards young people at work. Discuss the duties the Act places on employers.
questions.model: The Act sets a minimum age for full-time work and prevents children under 14 from working during school term. It limits the hours of young workers during term and holidays, and requires breaks and rest days. It restricts working late at night or early in the morning. Employers must obtain evidence of the young person's age and permission from a parent or guardian before employing them. Employers must keep a register of hours worked and pay young workers at the rate that applies to their age. Together these rules protect the health, safety and development of young people while allowing them to gain work experience.
